name: libev
workload: Socket-pair event loop benchmark (libev's bench.c): active clients exchanging data plus idle timers, scaled from 100 to 100,000 file descriptors with 100 and 1,000 active clients, measuring per-iteration dispatch time and timeout-handling overhead.
claimed_speedup: libev consistently 2-3x faster than libevent in the idle-timeout scenario across fd ranges; libevent took 'almost twice as much time' per iteration than libev without timeouts (libevent 1.4.3 vs libev 3.31, version 6 of the writeup, Jan 2011)
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars (GitHub mirror); historically used by Node.js (pre-libuv), Ruby, EventMachine, Tor
tradeoffs: More manual/lower-level API than libevent or libuv (explicit watcher structs, no built-in cross-platform abstraction beyond POSIX backends); weaker Windows support; author himself notes libevent 2.x (much newer than the 1.4.3 tested here) narrowed some gaps.
caveats: Benchmark dated Jan 2011 using old versions (libevent 1.4.3, libev 3.31); does not include libuv, which postdates this test and only appears in a separate, less rigorous third-party shootout (bartman/event-loop-benchmark) that itself cites this page as its methodology source and found libev/picoev still ahead of libuv on that author's machine, though without stated compiler flags or hardware.
found_via: gh search repos "event loop benchmark libuv libevent" -> bartman/event-loop-benchmark (comparing libev, libevent, libuev, libuv, picoev) -> its README cites libev.schmorp.de/bench.html as the original, more rigorous methodology

name: picoev
workload: Re-modified version of libev's bench.c measuring per-descriptor setup time and per-event processing time across scaling file-descriptor counts, for select/epoll/kqueue backends.
claimed_speedup: "it is faster than libevent or libev!" -- shown as two bar charts (setup time, event processing time) with picoev consistently lower/faster; no numeric values given in the README text, only in the linked chart images
tradeoffs: Only supports select(2)/epoll(2)/kqueue(2) (no IOCP); array-plus-bitvector-ring-buffer design gives only ~1-2s timeout granularity beyond 128 buckets; author explicitly states picoev is 'not comparable' to libevent/libev in maturity or feature set.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (unclear terms); benchmark charts are hosted as images (developer.cybozu.co.jp blog, itself old) with no numbers in text, no stated compiler or hardware; also appears as a top-two finisher (with libev) in the independent bartman/event-loop-benchmark shootout, which likewise lacks stated compiler flags/hardware.
found_via: gh search repos "event loop benchmark libuv libevent" -> bartman/event-loop-benchmark shootout lists picoev as a benchmarked contender that beat libevent/libuv on that author's machine; picoev's own README documents the same libevent/libev comparison

name: Seastar
workload: memaslap (libmemcached 1.0.18) GET/SET load against a Seastar-based, DPDK-backed memcached-protocol server vs stock Memcached 1.4.17 (libevent-based reactor, both multi-process and multi-threaded configurations), scaling from 2 to 20 CPU cores over a 40Gb NIC.
claimed_speedup: "SeaStar's Memcache server is 4X faster than the stock threaded memcache" and ~2x faster than the stock multi-process memcache; e.g. at 20 cores: Seastar+DPDK 4,426,457 ops/s vs stock multi-threaded 1,128,469 ops/s vs stock multi-process 2,281,064 ops/s
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2695v3 (2.3GHz base, 35MB cache, 14 cores each = 28 physical/56 HT per host), 64GB DDR4, dual Intel XL710-QDA1 40Gb NICs (hardware shared with the project's HTTPD-benchmark wiki page)
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars; core reactor engine of ScyllaDB
tradeoffs: Requires adopting Seastar's own future/promise async model and strict shard-per-core, share-nothing design (no implicit cross-core memory sharing); its highest numbers use a DPDK kernel-bypass network stack requiring hugepages and dedicated NICs, which is not a drop-in replacement for a plain epoll/libevent deployment; native TCP stack trades standard BSD-socket compatibility for speed.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (Seastar project's own GitHub wiki), not an independent third party; dated February 2015; compiler and build flags are not stated; the largest speedup (4x) is measured against memcached's threaded mode specifically, and the comparison is at the whole-application (memcached) level rather than a synthetic libevent-only microbenchmark, though memcached's own event loop is libevent-based.
found_via: gh search repos --topic event-loop / gh api repos/scylladb/seastar readme -> WebFetch seastar.io (redirects/links to project wiki) -> GitHub wiki pages 'Memcached Benchmark' and 'HTTPD benchmark'

name: gnet
workload: TCP echo-server benchmark with 1KB packets over tcpkali, at 1000/2000/5000/10000 concurrent connections on Linux, comparing gnet against Go's standard `net` package (its runtime netpoller wraps epoll on Linux), tidwall/evio, and CloudWeGo netpoll.
claimed_speedup: gnet had the highest QPS at every connection count vs. Go's std-net (epoll-based netpoller): 1000 conns 4,646,164 vs 3,250,189 (~1.4x, derived from chart data); 2000 conns 4,374,275 vs 2,371,727 (~1.8x, derived); 10000 conns 2,619,695 vs 1,343,247 (~1.95x, derived)
hardware: 8 CPU cores, AMD EPYC 7K62 48-Core Processor, 16GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04/x86_64
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; powers ByteDance's Kitex RPC framework and Hertz HTTP framework
tradeoffs: Event-driven callback model instead of Go's one-goroutine-per-connection blocking style, so migrating existing `net`-based code requires a rewrite; narrower feature surface than `net` (core TCP/UDP/Unix-socket only); author states gnet's TechEmpower HTTP entry is 'half-baked and fine-tuned for benchmark purposes only', not production-ready.
caveats: The actual numbers were read off a bar chart (image, not a table) in the linked gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks repo (39 stars, last updated 2024); the benchmark predates Go's netpoller improvements in newer releases (test used Go 1.17.2, ~2021) so the gap versus current Go `net` may differ; a companion TechEmpower Round 22 claim (gnet ranked #1 of 486 frameworks) is also chart-only and not independently reproduced here.
found_via: gh search --topic event-loop -> panjf2000/gnet README 'Performance' -> Contrasts to similar networking libraries (On Linux/epoll) -> linked gnet-io/gnet-benchmarks repo

name: uvloop
workload: Echo-server benchmark exercising asyncio's low-level socket API (loop.sock_recv/sock_sendall), high-level streams API (asyncio.start_server), and the protocol API (loop.create_server), at 1/10/100 KiB message sizes, comparing stock asyncio's default epoll-based SelectorEventLoop against uvloop (a libuv-backed loop swapped in via asyncio.set_event_loop_policy).
claimed_speedup: README states 'uvloop makes asyncio 2-4x faster'; chart data shows e.g. protocol API at 1KiB: ~107k uvloop vs ~43k asyncio req/s (~2.5x, derived from chart); sockets API at 1KiB: ~52k uvloop vs ~13.5k asyncio req/s (~3.9x, derived from chart)
tradeoffs: Adds a compiled C-extension (Cython + vendored libuv) build/install dependency instead of the pure-Python stdlib loop; historically Linux/macOS-focused with weaker Windows story; some asyncio edge cases (e.g. certain subprocess/signal behaviors) have lagged the stdlib implementation over time.
caveats: The magic.io blog post that originally accompanied this chart (linked from the README) no longer resolves (DNS failure at fetch time), so the exact hardware and Python version used are unconfirmed; all numbers here were read directly off the bar chart image, not from text; the chart appears old (predates uvloop's current Python 3.8+ requirement).
found_via: gh search repos --topic event-loop -> MagicStack/uvloop README 'Performance' section -> performance.png chart
